W: Hello, I'm calling about the two-room flat on Amir Temur Street. Is it still available?
M: Yes, it is. It's on the fourth floor, fully furnished, with a new kitchen.
W: Great. How much is the rent?
M: It's four hundred and fifty dollars a month... no, wait, I do apologise — the owner raised it last week, so it's four hundred and eighty now, including utilities.
W: I see. Could I come and view it tomorrow evening?
M: Of course. Shall we say six o'clock?

Two.
W: Good afternoon. Do you have anything for a sore throat?
M: These lozenges are very effective. And if you also have a fever, I'd recommend these tablets.
W: How should I take the tablets?
M: One tablet twice a day — in the morning and in the evening. Make sure you take them after meals, never on an empty stomach.
W: So one before breakfast and one before dinner?
M: No — after eating, please. Otherwise they can upset your stomach.
W: Understood. Thank you.

Three.
M: Are you coming to the match on Sunday? It's Pakhtakor against Nasaf.
W: Definitely! What time does it start?
M: Kick-off is at seven in the evening. Let's meet outside the west gate at six.
W: Six o'clock... the traffic on Sunday evenings is terrible, though.
M: You're right. Let's make it half past five instead — then we'll have time to find our seats.
W: Perfect. Half past five at the west gate.

Four.
W: Hello, this is Tech Service calling about the laptop you brought in yesterday.
M: Oh, good. Did you find the problem? I thought the battery was dying.
W: At first we suspected the battery too, but after testing everything it turned out to be the cooling fan. It's completely blocked with dust, so the laptop overheats and switches itself off.
M: I see. How much will the repair cost?
W: Cleaning and a new fan will be a hundred and fifty thousand soums, and it'll be ready on Thursday.
M: That's fine. Thank you.

Five.
M: Hello, City Taxi? I need a car to the international airport tomorrow morning.
W: Certainly. What time is your flight?
M: It leaves at seven fifteen, so I'd like to be at the airport by half past five.
W: Then we'll pick you up at a quarter to five. What's your address?
M: Twelve, Bobur Street, apartment eight — the entrance is at the back of the building.
W: A quarter to five, twelve Bobur Street. The driver will call you when he arrives.

Six.
W: Timur! I'm so glad I caught you. My sister is getting married next Saturday, and we'd love you to come.
M: Congratulations! Of course I'll come. Where's the ceremony?
W: The wedding party will be at the Navruz restaurant, near the city park. It starts at five in the evening.
M: Should I bring anything?
W: Just yourself! Oh — and it would be lovely if you could take some photos. You're so good with your camera.
M: With pleasure.

Seven.
M: Good morning, Star Language Centre.
W: Hi, I'd like to join your English course. I saw the advert for the evening group.
M: The evening group meets on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays at seven o'clock.
W: Hmm, that's a problem — I work late shifts on Fridays. Do you have anything at the weekend?
M: We do — the weekend group meets on Saturday and Sunday mornings at ten.
W: That suits me much better. Can I register for that one, please?
M: Of course. I just need your name and a copy of your passport.

Eight.
M: Dilnoza, I missed Professor Rahimov's lecture on Tuesday — I was at the dentist's. Could I copy your notes?
W: To be honest, my notes are a mess. But don't worry — the professor uploads his slides to the university portal after every lecture.
M: Really? I didn't know that.
W: And this time he even recorded the whole lecture on video, because half the group was away at the sports competition. Just log in and watch it.
M: That's brilliant. I'll do that tonight. Thanks!

Talk one. University orientation announcement.
W: Good morning, everyone, and a very warm welcome to Tashkent International University! Before you rush off to explore, let me run through today's programme. The welcome meeting for all first-year students begins at nine o'clock sharp in the Main Hall — that's on the ground floor of Building A, straight through the glass doors. The rector will speak first, followed by the heads of each faculty. As soon as the meeting finishes, please make your way to the library, where staff will be waiting to hand out your student ID cards. Don't forget to bring your passport, or they won't be able to give you the card. You'll need the ID for the canteen, the buses and, of course, for borrowing books. Then, in the afternoon, at two o'clock, our student volunteers will take you on a guided tour of the campus — the sports centre, the computer labs, the dormitories, everything. The tour starts from the fountain in front of the Main Hall. One more thing: free Wi-Fi is available everywhere on campus, and you'll find the password printed on the back of your welcome pack. Enjoy your first day!

Talk two. Swimming pool rules.
M: Right, before we open the pool to our new members, let me quickly go over the safety rules — please listen carefully. First of all, everyone must take a shower before entering the water. This is not optional; it keeps the pool clean for all of us. Second, swimming caps are compulsory in every lane. If you haven't got one, don't worry — you can buy a cap at the reception desk for just fifteen thousand soums. Third, children under twelve must be accompanied by an adult at all times, both in the water and around the pool. The floor gets slippery, so no running, please. And finally, opening hours: on weekdays the pool closes at half past nine in the evening, and at the weekend we close an hour earlier. Any questions? No? Then enjoy your swim!

context.transcript:
M: Welcome back to Health Matters, the podcast that separates science from nonsense. My guest today is Dr. Lola Karimova, a nutritionist with fifteen years of clinical experience. Doctor, food myths are everywhere. Why do they spread so quickly?
W: Mostly because of social media. Anyone with a camera can call themselves a nutrition expert, and dramatic claims get far more clicks than careful scientific facts. Real research is complicated and full of 'maybes', but a slogan like 'sugar is poison' takes three seconds to share.
M: Let's test a few myths, then. Number one: breakfast is the most important meal of the day, and skipping it is dangerous.
W: That's simply not true for everyone. For some people breakfast is genuinely helpful — children, for example, concentrate better after it. But recent studies show that healthy adults who prefer to skip it come to no harm at all. What matters is the total amount and quality of food you eat across the whole day, not the clock on the wall.
M: Myth number two: eating carbohydrates after six in the evening makes you gain weight.
W: Another favourite of mine — and another myth. Your body doesn't keep a timetable. Weight gain happens when you regularly eat more calories than you burn. It makes very little difference whether you eat your rice at midday or at eight in the evening.
M: And what about detox juices? They're everywhere at the moment.
W: Honestly? They're a waste of money. Your liver and your kidneys already remove unwanted substances from your body every second of every day — that is their job, and they are very good at it. No juice can do it better. In fact, some of these fashionable drinks contain more sugar than a bottle of cola.
M: Strong words! So what's your advice to our listeners?
W: Before you believe any claim about food, check who is making it. Ask whether the person has a real qualification and whether serious research supports what they say. And remember — no single food is magic. Variety and moderation are what keep us healthy, boring as that sounds.
M: Dr. Karimova, thank you very much.

parts.instructionsUz: Xotira qanday ishlashi va samarali o'qish usullari haqidagi ma'ruzaning bir qismini eshitasiz. 30-35-savollar uchun to'g'ri javobni tanlang.

context.transcript: M: Good afternoon, everyone. Today's lecture is about how memory works — and how you can use that knowledge to study far more effectively. When you learn something new, the information first enters your short-term memory. This store is surprisingly small and fragile: it holds around seven items for about a minute — actually, let me correct myself, recent research suggests it's even less than that: no more than thirty seconds, unless you actively repeat the information. If you do nothing with it, it simply disappears. A German psychologist called Hermann Ebbinghaus demonstrated this more than a century ago. He showed that within just a few days we forget most of what we have learned — unless we review it. His famous graph is known as the forgetting curve. So how do we move knowledge into long-term memory? The single most effective technique, confirmed by hundreds of studies, is spaced repetition: reviewing material at increasing intervals — after a day, then a week, then a month. Each review at the right moment makes the memory stronger and slower to fade. Testing yourself works for the same reason: the effort of pulling information out of your memory strengthens it far more than passively looking at it again. And that brings me to a very common mistake. Many students prepare for exams by rereading their notes and highlighting them the night before. It feels productive, but the research is clear: rereading creates only an illusion of knowledge — the text looks familiar, so you believe you know it, when in fact you don't. Finally, whatever you do, don't sacrifice your sleep. During deep sleep, the brain replays the day's experiences and transfers important information from short-term into long-term storage. A student who sleeps eight hours after studying remembers significantly more the next morning than one who stays up all night cramming. In short: space your reviews, test yourself, and go to bed. Next week we'll look at how emotion affects what we remember.

parts.passageText:
The Rise of Electric Cars

A. Many people imagine that electric cars are a twenty-first-century invention. In fact, at the beginning of the 1900s electric vehicles were more popular in American cities than petrol ones: they were quiet, clean and easy to drive. It was only when cheap petrol and mass-produced models like the Ford Model T arrived that electric cars almost disappeared from the roads for a hundred years.

B. The heart of every modern electric car is its battery, and this is where progress has been fastest. Twenty years ago batteries were heavy, expensive and offered a range of barely one hundred kilometres. Today's lithium-ion packs cost a fraction of the price and can power a family car for four or five hundred kilometres on a single charge — and researchers promise that the next generation of solid-state batteries will go even further.

C. Supporters point out that electric cars produce no exhaust fumes, which could dramatically improve air quality in crowded cities. However, scientists remind us that an electric car is only as clean as the electricity it runs on. In countries that burn coal to generate power, the environmental advantage becomes much smaller. The greenest electric car is one charged with energy from the sun, the wind or water.

D. Price remains a serious obstacle for many families. A new electric model usually costs noticeably more than a similar petrol car. On the other hand, owners spend far less on fuel and maintenance, because electric motors have very few moving parts. Many governments also offer subsidies, free parking or tax reductions, so over several years the total cost of ownership can actually turn out to be lower.

E. Perhaps the biggest practical problem is where to charge. Drivers with a private garage can simply plug in overnight, but millions of people live in blocks of flats. Long queues at motorway charging stations during the holidays show that infrastructure has not kept up with sales. Experts warn that without hundreds of thousands of new public chargers, the growth of electric driving will slow down.

F. Despite these difficulties, most analysts believe the direction of travel is clear. Several European countries plan to ban the sale of new petrol and diesel cars by 2035, and major manufacturers have announced that their future models will be fully electric. If battery prices continue to fall, the electric car may dominate our roads within a generation.

parts.passageText:
Honeybees and Why They Matter

When people think of honeybees, they usually think of honey. Yet the sweet liquid in our tea is actually the least important thing these insects give us. Around one third of the food on our plates — including apples, cherries, cucumbers, almonds and melons — depends on pollination, the process by which bees carry pollen from one flower to another so that plants can produce fruit and seeds. Scientists estimate that the work done by bees and other pollinators is worth more than 150 billion dollars to the world economy every year.

A single honeybee colony is a remarkable society of up to sixty thousand individuals, almost all of them female workers. Each worker changes jobs as she grows older: she begins by cleaning the hive and feeding the young, later guards the entrance, and only in the final weeks of her life flies out to collect nectar and pollen. To produce one kilogram of honey, the bees of a hive together fly a distance roughly equal to three times around the Earth.

Communication inside the colony is equally impressive. When a worker discovers a rich source of flowers, she performs a special 'waggle dance' on the honeycomb. The direction and length of the dance tell her sisters exactly where the flowers are — a discovery that won the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch a Nobel Prize in 1973.

Worryingly, bee populations have been falling in many parts of the world for two decades, and researchers do not blame a single cause. Chemical pesticides weaken bees' memory and navigation; parasites such as the Varroa mite spread deadly viruses; and modern farming replaces wildflower meadows with endless fields of a single crop, leaving bees with a poor and monotonous diet. Climate change adds further stress by confusing the timing of flowering.

The good news is that everyone can help. Planting flowers rich in nectar — lavender, sunflowers or simple wildflowers — provides food for bees in towns and cities. Buying honey from local beekeepers supports the people who care for colonies, and even leaving a corner of a garden wild makes a difference. City authorities are joining in too: Paris, London and Tashkent now host thousands of urban hives on rooftops and in parks. Interestingly, studies show that city bees are often healthier than their country cousins, thanks to the greater variety of flowers in parks and on balconies and the lower use of agricultural chemicals.

Volunteering Changed My Life

Two years ago I was a typical second-year student: lectures in the morning, computer games in the evening, and a quiet feeling that something was missing. [15] At first I ignored it, telling myself that volunteering was for people with too much free time.

A month later my best friend dragged me along to the centre's open day. [16] Instead, I met engineers, doctors and grandmothers, all sorting donated books for village schools with enormous enthusiasm.

That same week I signed up for the weekend literacy project. My job was to read stories to children at a local orphanage. [17] My hands were shaking and I forgot half the story. But the children didn't care — they begged me to come back the following week.

Little by little, those visits became the best part of my week. [18] For example, I learned to explain difficult words simply, to listen patiently, and to stay calm when twenty children are all talking at once.

The biggest surprise, though, came at university. [19] My marks actually improved because, for the first time in my life, I was managing my time instead of wasting it.

Last spring the centre asked me to coordinate a new team of fifteen volunteers. [20] Leading people turned out to be the hardest and most rewarding thing I had ever done.

Looking back, I realise that the person who benefited most from my volunteering was me. [21] If you are hesitating the way I was, my advice is simple: go to that open day. You have nothing to lose except a few free evenings — and so much to gain.

parts.passageText:
Is Social Media Making Us Lonely?

We have never been so connected — and, if we believe the headlines, never so lonely. The average teenager now spends over four hours a day on social platforms, collecting friends, followers and likes by the hundred. Yet in survey after survey, young people report feeling more isolated than any generation before them. Is the technology that promised to bring us together actually pushing us apart?

The pessimists have some powerful evidence. Psychologists point out that scrolling through other people's carefully edited highlights — the holidays, the parties, the perfect breakfasts — invites us to compare our ordinary lives with an impossible standard. Comparison, not connection, is the default activity on many platforms. One influential American study found that the more time participants spent on social media, the worse they felt afterwards; face-to-face contact had exactly the opposite effect.

There is also the question of what online contact replaces. An evening spent exchanging comments with strangers is an evening not spent having dinner with family or walking with a friend. Sociologists call this 'displacement', and it worries them most in the case of teenagers, whose social skills are still developing. If you learn to end every awkward conversation by simply closing an app, how do you ever learn to repair a real friendship after an argument?

And yet the story is not so simple. For many people, online communities are a lifeline rather than a substitute. A teenager with a rare illness, a young mother at home with a baby, a student who has moved to a city where she knows nobody — for them, a phone can be the difference between isolation and belonging. Research increasingly suggests that how we use social media matters far more than how much. People who actively message friends, plan meetings and join groups tend to feel more connected; those who silently scroll through strangers' photos tend to feel worse.

My own view is that social media is neither a disease nor a cure, but a mirror — one that exaggerates whatever we bring to it. A sociable person uses it to arrange picnics; a lonely person uses it to watch other people's picnics. Blaming the platforms for loneliness is comfortable, because it saves us from asking harder questions about long working hours, disappearing public spaces and neighbourhoods where nobody knows anybody. Smartphones did not create human loneliness, and deleting an app will not end it. The real challenge is to treat these tools as a bridge to real contact rather than a replacement for it — and to be honest with ourselves about which of the two we are actually doing.

parts.passageText:
The Psychology of First Impressions

How long does it take to form an opinion of a stranger? According to research carried out at Princeton University, considerably less time than most people imagine. When psychologists Janine Willis and Alexander Todorov showed participants photographs of unfamiliar faces, judgements about trustworthiness, competence and attractiveness were made after an exposure of just one tenth of a second. Longer viewing times did not change these first judgements; they merely increased the participants' confidence in them.

Such speed suggests that first impressions are not careful decisions but automatic processes, inherited from a distant past in which an instant reading of friend or enemy could decide survival. The brain region most involved, the amygdala, reacts to faces before we are even conscious of seeing them. In evolutionary terms, a system that produced fast, roughly accurate guesses was more useful than a slow, perfectly fair one.

The trouble is that the modern world punishes this ancient shortcut. Studies consistently show that adults with 'baby faces' — round cheeks and large eyes — are judged to be warmer but less competent, and are less likely to be promoted to senior positions, although there is no evidence that they perform worse. Similarly, taller candidates enjoy measurable advantages in job interviews and even in elections. Interviewers who feel they are objectively assessing a candidate's answers are often, in reality, defending a verdict reached in the first ninety seconds of the meeting — a tendency psychologists call confirmation bias: the habit of noticing evidence that supports what we already believe and overlooking evidence that contradicts it.

Can a bad first impression be repaired? The news is mixed. Experiments indicate that negative first impressions are considerably more resistant to change than positive ones, apparently because threatening information receives priority in memory. On average, participants needed to observe around eight instances of positive behaviour before they revised an initial negative judgement of a person — while a single negative act was often enough to destroy a positive one. Psychologists refer to this asymmetry as negativity bias.

Nevertheless, first impressions are not destiny. Awareness of the process appears to weaken its power: interviewers trained to delay their judgement, to use structured questions and to score answers against written criteria make measurably fairer decisions. Some orchestras discovered this decades ago. When they began holding 'blind' auditions, with musicians performing behind a screen, the proportion of women hired rose dramatically — clear evidence of how much irrelevant visual information had been influencing supposedly expert judgements.

The practical lesson is twofold. When meeting others, we should remember that our instant verdicts are guesses, not knowledge, and give people a genuine second chance. And when being met — at an interview, or on a first day at work — it is worth accepting the reality of the shortcut: arrive on time, smile, and pay attention to the details, because the judgement made in that first tenth of a second will be defended, often unconsciously, for a long time afterwards.

questions.promptEn: In the Princeton experiment, what was the effect of longer viewing times?

options: People became more certain of judgements they had already made
People completely changed their first judgements
People refused to judge the faces at all
People remembered the faces less accurately

answer.value: People became more certain of judgements they had already made

answer.value: Quick decisions about strangers once helped survival

answer.value: Noticing mainly the evidence that supports an existing opinion

answer.value: A much higher proportion of women were hired

questions.promptEn:
You received this email from your friend Emma:

"Hi! Great news — we're organising a picnic by Charvak lake this Saturday: swimming, barbecue, volleyball, the lot! Everyone's meeting at the bus station at 11 am. You're coming, right? Let me know! Emma"

Write a reply to Emma. In your email: thank her for the invitation; explain why you cannot come on Saturday; suggest meeting at another time. Write at least 50 words.

You saw this announcement on an international website:

"GREEN SUMMER — International Volunteer Programme. Spend four weeks abroad helping real environmental projects: tree planting, river clean-ups, wildlife protection. Accommodation provided. For further information contact the programme coordinator, Ms Sarah Collins."
